opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the brain is a useful source of inspiration here, though I'd be a little careful about taking the analogy too literally.

The thing that strikes me most is that the brain doesn't run one big sequential loop where it perceives, then thinks, then acts. Lots of things happen at once and at different timescales. Your spinal cord and lower-level motor circuits handle fast reflexive corrections. Higher-level areas deal with slower things like planning, figuring out what goal you're pursuing, and reasoning about the scene. They all run concurrently and talk to each other continuously.

Most robotic systems today, including a lot of the vision-language-action models we and others have been building, are still fairly synchronous. You take an observation, run a big network, get an action or a chunk of actions, execute, and repeat. That works surprisingly well, but it creates a real tension. If you want the model to be smart, with lots of semantic knowledge from internet-scale pretraining and the ability to reason about what it's doing, it has to be big, and big models are slow. But physical interaction needs fast, reactive control. When you're folding a shirt and the fabric slips, you can't wait half a second to think about it.

So one lesson I'd take from the brain is to stop treating the problem as one monolithic inference step. Instead, you have a system where a slower, more deliberative component sets context and intent while a faster component handles the moment-to-moment motor control. Crucially, they run in parallel and asynchronously rather than taking turns. We've seen hints of this already. Systems that separate a high-level "what should I do next" process from a low-level action-generating process, or that let the robot keep acting while the next chunk is being computed, tend to be much smoother and more robust.

The other piece, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the brain is doing perception, prediction, and action all at once, and they're deeply intertwined. You're constantly predicting what your hand will feel before it touches something. That kind of continuous prediction gives you a rich learning signal and makes you robust to surprises. For embodied AI, it suggests that our models shouldn't just map observations to actions. They should also be modeling what's going to happen, at multiple levels of abstraction, simultaneously.

That said, I'd be cautious about trying to copy the brain's specific architecture. We don't fully understand it, and our hardware is very different: GPUs are good at big, dense, batched computation, not billions of tiny asynchronous units. So the useful takeaway is the principles, not the wiring diagram. Have multiple timescales, run them concurrently, let fast reactive control coexist with slower reasoning, and keep prediction in the loop. If we get those principles right with the tools we have, I think we'll get robots that feel much more fluid and capable, and less like they're stopping to think between every movement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being a little careful here, because "parallel processing" can mean a few different things, and the brain is interesting for reasons that go beyond just the fact that it's massively parallel. I mean, GPUs are massively parallel too, and that by itself doesn't get you a robot that can fold laundry.

But I think there are a couple of lessons that are genuinely relevant for embodied systems. The first is that the brain isn't running a single serial loop of "perceive, think, act." You have a lot of things happening at different timescales simultaneously. There's very fast reflexive control happening in the spinal cord and brainstem, there's intermediate-level sensorimotor stuff, and then there's slower deliberative processing. And critically, these are running at the same time, and the slow stuff doesn't have to finish before the fast stuff can respond. If you're about to drop a glass, your hand adjusts before you've consciously registered that anything happened.

For a robot, that's actually a very practical design consideration. A lot of our systems today still have this bottleneck where you run a big model, you get an action, you execute it, you run the model again. And if the model is large, which the good ones are, that imposes a pretty severe constraint on how reactive you can be. So one direction people are exploring, and we've looked at this too, is having a hierarchy where a big model is reasoning about what to do at a coarse level, and something faster and lighter is actually closing the loop with the world. The big model doesn't need to be in the critical path for every single motor command. It needs to be providing the right context to something that is.

The second lesson, which I think is actually more subtle, is that in the brain, perception and action aren't really separate modules that pass messages to each other. They're deeply intertwined. The way you perceive the world is shaped by what you're trying to do, and your actions are constantly generating the sensory data that drives learning. So I'd be a little cautious about taking "parallel processing" to mean "build a bunch of independent modules and run them side by side." I think the more interesting version is that you have a system where many things are being computed jointly, and the boundaries between perception, prediction, and control are kind of blurry.

And honestly, that's one of the arguments for end-to-end learning in robotics. If you let the network figure out the representation, it tends to discover that the right features for perception are the ones that are useful for acting, and that coupling is something you'd have a very hard time engineering by hand.

The last thing I'd say is just a note of caution. I think a lot of the time when people look to the brain for inspiration, they end up with analogies that sound nice but don't actually change what you build. The thing that has consistently worked in machine learning is scale, data, and fairly simple general-purpose architectures. So I'd want the neuroscience inspiration to cash out in something concrete: a different training objective, a different way of structuring the latency of the system, something like that. The high-level principle that "the brain does a lot at once" is true, but it's the specific structure of what runs fast versus slow, and what gets learned versus hard-coded, that I think actually matters for robots.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that the brain has to solve a lot of problems simultaneously. When you’re having this conversation, you’re also maintaining your posture, processing what you see, and controlling your movements. You don’t appear to be doing that by running one conscious reasoning process that decides, in sequence, what every muscle should do.

For embodied AI, that suggests an architecture where different processes operate at different timescales. If a robot is carrying a glass of water, it might reason relatively slowly about where to put it, while a much faster controller makes adjustments to keep it stable. You wouldn’t want every adjustment to require a whole new round of deliberation.

But I’d be cautious about taking that as a prescription to hand-design a separate module for every function. The hard question is how those processes learn together and exchange information. Your plan has to reflect what your motor system can actually execute, and your motor system has to respond to changes in the plan.

So the lesson I’d take is less about copying the brain’s anatomy and more about allowing learned behavior to operate concurrently, with feedback at multiple timescales. Then the question is: what training procedure makes that whole system work coherently?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that the brain has to solve a lot of problems simultaneously. While you're talking to somebody, you're also maintaining your posture, processing what you see, and controlling where you look. You're not consciously scheduling each of those operations in sequence.

For robots, we often build systems that are much more sequential: first perceive the world, then make a plan, then execute the plan. But the world keeps changing while you're doing that. So there's a lot to be gained from having processes operating concurrently, at different timescales. You might have a slower process deciding what you're trying to accomplish, while a faster process continuously adjusts your movements based on sensory feedback.

The difficult question is how those processes coordinate and how you train them together. Having a bunch of parallel modules doesn't automatically give you intelligent behavior. They need to share information and learn in a way that makes their contributions useful to the overall task. I think that's where studying the brain can provide inspiration, without necessarily requiring us to reproduce its architecture exactly.
